sections.heading: Lighting, Pose and the Rules That Get Photos Approved
paragraphs: Official photo guidelines converge on the same principles across most countries: facing the camera, neutral expression, mouth closed and eyes open and clearly visible. Glasses must be free of glare, and head coverings are permitted only for religious reasons that are declared to the interviewer or service.

Lighting should fall evenly on the face with no shadows behind you, and the background must be a plain solid color without textures. Wearing clothing that contrasts with the background prevents your outline from disappearing into the image.

Reviewing each official guideline before taking the shot saves a rejected application, and the tool positions your crop within the required head-height and face-width proportions that scanners expect.

sections.heading: Printing at the Correct Physical Size
paragraphs: A digital photo that looks correct on screen can still be rejected if it prints at the wrong physical dimensions. Passport photo booths and application offices require specifics like 35 by 45 mm for many passport types or 2 by 2 inches for US passports.

Setting the correct pixels-per-inch value matters because a file that is exactly 600 by 600 pixels prints at 1 inch when saved at 600 PPI but at 2 inches when saved at 300 PPI. Choosing a print-ready export keeps the math consistent.

When an application office prints your photos, the file must also preserve enough resolution that the face remains sharp at the required print size. Exporting at a resolution that satisfies both the pixel dimensions and the physical print size removes the final rejection risk.

sections.heading: Expiry Renewal and Consistency Across Documents
paragraphs: Renewing a passport or updating a work badge calls for a fresh photo that still reads as the same person across all your documents. Keeping one current portrait as the reference and regenerating compliant crops from it makes every new card recognizably yours.

Consistency matters for verification: border systems and HR databases compare new photos against stored biometric references, and a photo that obviously resembles your existing records clears checks faster.

Preparing the digital file at the correct size means you can submit electronically exactly as required, while simultaneously printing a sheet in the physical size for offices that still request paper.
